title: Y-chromosome lineages and surnames, two blurry trails
Who is Responsible for Tackling Professional Deskilling?
abstract: Abstract There has been increasing interest across several professional fields in problems of deskilling , that is, the loss or the lack of development of human skills due to outsourcing tasks to artificial intelligence. Avigail Ferdman (“AI Deskilling is a Structural Problem.” AI & Society 41 (4): 3001–13, 2026) has recently argued that deskilling should be seen as a structural problem. In this paper, based on empirical literature on the relevant heuristics and biases, I present a novel empirically-informed philosophical argument as to why this seems to be the case. According to the empirical literature on deskilling, automation bias, and skill decay, many professionals rely on artificial intelligence much more than is necessary when it is available, and the effects of such overreliance on skill decay are unlikely to be entirely understood by the professionals themselves. I argue that this – what I call the insidious nature of deskilling – supports a normative view, according to which the responsibility for tackling deskilling should not be ascribed to the individual professional but the risks of professional deskilling should be tackled by the professional community instead. Mitigating the risks of deskilling should start from an intra-field analysis of the core skills of the profession that should not be outsourced to artificial intelligence. Then, the individual professional would not be left alone to determine how and when to prevent deskilling during the adoption of artificial intelligence within her profession.

title: When awareness backfires: activation and attenuation in fast fashion ethics
abstract: Purpose This study aims to address a persistent paradox in sustainable fashion: why rising consumer awareness of fast fashion’s environmental and labour harms fails to produce durable attitudinal resistance, particularly in structurally high-saturation, high-exposure market environments characterised by dense media intensity, accelerated trend cycles, and persistent sustainability discourse. Design/methodology/approach A three-wave longitudinal survey of fast-fashion consumers in East and Southeast Asia was conducted. Latent growth curve modelling and random-intercept cross-lagged panel models were applied to isolate within-person change and examine dynamic mediation and boundary-conditioned trajectories. Findings Dark-side awareness activates perceived risk and moral concern at early exposure stages, strengthening attitudinal resistance, but these effects attenuate as exposure accumulates. Risk appraisal and moral concern function as time-sensitive transmission mechanisms with declining marginal influence. Information saturation accelerates attenuation, generating non-monotonic resistance trajectories characterised by activation, plateau, and reversal. Originality/value This study advances a theory-revising contribution by reconceptualising consumer awareness as a dynamic moral regulation process rather than a stable antecedent. It challenges linear escalation assumptions embedded in sustainable consumption research and demonstrates that repeated exposure can suppress, rather than amplify, ethical resistance. By evidencing non-monotonic awareness effects in market environments defined by structurally high media intensity, accelerated trend cycles, and dense sustainability discourse, the study establishes temporal adaptation as a core explanatory mechanism absent from dominant cross-sectional models.

title: What role does healthcare geographic accessibility play in the association between personal health responsibility and family doctor contract services?
Understanding food quality labels in complex markets. The role of heuristics in consumer decision-making
journal: International Journal of Quality & Reliability Management
abstract: Purpose This study examines how consumers interpret differentiated food quality labels in complex markets, focusing on cognitive accessibility and heuristics to explain why signals such as local origin can outweigh formal or technically complex certifications. Design/methodology/approach The article combines bibliometric analysis with a qualitative scoping review. A corpus of 510 publications from 1996–2026 was analysed using science-mapping techniques, followed by a cluster-guided synthesis of evidence on label proliferation, consumer interpretation, willingness to pay and territorial outcomes. Findings The literature has shifted from information provision and attitudes towards the economic valuation of sustainability attributes. The synthesis identifies label overload, attention competition, cue substitution, hypothetical bias and divergence between consumer valuation and territorial outcomes. Local origin often functions as an accessible cue bundling authenticity, trust, freshness and community support, which can increase its influence relative to more complex certifications. Practical implications Regulators, certification bodies and firms should assess overlap before adding labels, organise information hierarchically and combine credible verification with intuitive design. Consumer education should clarify what accessible claims such as “local” do and do not guarantee. Originality/value The study develops a multi-label heuristic framework distinguishing technical credibility from cognitive accessibility and specifying how their relative influence changes with label density. It integrates insights on trust, comprehension, label proliferation and heuristic choice to explain cross-label substitution, local-cue dominance and sub-additive valuation.

title: Trade fairs as relational network spaces: catalysing sustainable innovation. A study in the footwear industrial network
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to investigate how trade fairs (TFs), conceptualised as relational network spaces (RNS), catalyse sustainable innovation (SI) through changes in business relationship dynamics. It investigates how interactions at TFs stimulate SI at three analytical levels: firm, relationship and network, within the context of an industry facing increasing sustainability pressures. Design/methodology/approach Anchored in the Industrial Marketing and Purchasing perspective, this qualitative case study draws on semi-structured interviews and secondary data from the Portuguese footwear industry. A multi-level analysis is used to trace how TF-driven interactions reshape firms’ capabilities, inter-organisational ties and network dynamics in ways that support SI. Findings The study reveals that TFs act as multi-level catalysts for SI through three interrelated change processes: learning and reorienting at the firm level, accessing and connecting at the relationship level and collaborating and acting collectively at the network level. As temporary RNS, TFs create structural, relative and relational conditions that intensify interaction, enable access to sustainability-oriented actors, reshape existing relationships and support collective mobilisation around sustainability goals. SI emerges as a co-constructed and cumulative process unfolding across multiple actors and levels over time. Originality/value This study contributes to business network research by integrating space, process and time to explain how temporary interaction contexts generate enduring relational and innovation outcomes. It advances SI literature by conceptualising SI as a co-constructed, emergent, multi-level process shaped through business relationship dynamics. It also extends TF research by reframing TFs as relational infrastructures that actively support sustainability transitions.

title: Towards climate-resilient sustainable development: GIS-based multi-criteria flood risk assessment using Fuzzy-AHP in the Indian Sundarbans
Outside the box
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to review the latest management developments across the globe and pinpoint practical implications from cutting-edge research and case studies. Design/methodology/approach This briefing is prepared by an independent writer who adds their own impartial comments and places the articles in context. Findings This paper identified that informality and power imbalances are central within global value chains and can influence different outcomes for participating entities. Originality/value The briefing saves busy executives, strategists and researchers hours of reading time by selecting only the very best, most pertinent information and presenting it in a condensed and easy-to-digest format.
